title: Constructive Distortion: Improving MLLMs with Attention-Guided Image Warping
claim: Reallocating resolution toward query-relevant regions via attention-derived warping lets the same model correct an answer it previously got wrong.
layout: Single row, left-to-right: original image and wrong answer, attention aggregation, central attention-matrix panel with marginal bars, warping, warped image and correct answer; arrows carry stage labels
description: A horizontal flow from left to right. On the left is a question ("On the right desk, what is to the left of the laptop?") above a room photo with a green box around a lamp and laptop. Under it, a red box with a robot icon shows LLaVA's wrong answer (a stack of books). An arrow labeled "Attention Aggregation from Language Decoder" points to a uniform grid and then into a rounded central panel. The panel holds a heatmap over the photo, called the attention score matrix, with blue bar charts along the top and right edges for the marginal profiles. A second arrow labeled "Rectilinear Warping" leads to a warped grid, shown as a red-blue heatmap with a dense center. Next to it is the warped image, where the lamp and laptop region is enlarged. A green box with a robot icon below gives the correct answer (a lamp). The eye goes first to the central heatmap, then to the red and green answer boxes.
caption: \ourmethodshort overview. Given a query, our method extracts cross-modal attention maps from the MLLM's language decoder, aggregates them into marginal attention profiles, and uses rectilinear warping to expand high-attention regions while compressing low-attention areas. The warped image is then processed by the same MLLM, which now produces the correct answer.
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss small details and spatial relations in cluttered scenes, leading to errors in fine-grained perceptual grounding. We introduce AttWarp, a lightweight method that allocates more resolution to query-relevant content while compressing less informative areas, all while preserving global context. At test time, the approach uses an MLLM's cross-modal attention to perform rectilinear warping of the input image, reallocating spatial resolution toward regions the model deems important, without changing model weights or architecture. This attention-guided warping preserves all original image information but redistributes it non-uniformly, so small objects and subtle relationships become easier for the same model to read while the global layout remains intact. Across five benchmarks (TextVQA, GQA, DocVQA, POPE, MMMU) and four MLLMs (LLaVA, Qwen-VL, InternVL, and InstructBLIP), AttWarp consistently improves accuracy, strengthens compositional reasoning, and reduces hallucinations, outperforming four competitive baselines that manipulate raw images at test time. Together, these results show that attention-guided warping prioritizes information relevant to the query while preserving context, and that the same MLLMs perform better when given such warped inputs.
